A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SecureVibeBench, with the same 105-task benchmark, construction pipeline and agent evaluation. Text, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original agent evaluations, correctness/security rates, cost and time analyses, and manual assessment of SAST false alarms.

after.justification: Sections 4–5 retain those original empirical results, and Appendix E adds interaction-trace and patch-analysis evidence.

M1.justification: The B-SZZ candidate search, PoV verification of vulnerability boundaries, requirement processing, differential testing and Semgrep evaluation remain unchanged. The new diagrams and filtering examples explain the existing procedure; no algorithm or agent modification is reported.

E1.justification: Both evaluate 105 C/C++ tasks from the same 41 OSS-Fuzz/ARVO projects. The new nine-domain categorization describes existing projects, and the added case studies examine retained benchmark tasks. No new dataset, language or evaluation scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: Both retain the same 15 combinations of SWE-agent, OpenHands and Aider with five backbone models, plus Codex with GPT-5 and Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 4.5. Appendix C newly explains Agentless's exclusion; it is not an added evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The evaluation oracles, outcome categories, Semgrep configuration and agent settings match, including temperature 0 and the 75-iteration/$2 limits for SWE-agent and OpenHands. The revised CWE-percentage explanation clarifies aggregation over generated patches without establishing a changed metric or testing procedure.

E4.justification: Appendix E expands the previously reported task 58663 context-exhaustion failure with a trajectory, adds chat-history analysis of the existing rawspeed 5296 patch contrast, and introduces an agent–human patch comparison for task 22110. These are limited case-study additions; the aggregate failure and SAST analyses already existed.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 still states that each combination is run once. Neither version reports repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests for its own agent results. The new warning about possible statistical instability is a limitation, not a new statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The main result charts and Tables 2–4 retain their numerical values, including the best C-SEC rate of 23.8%. Section 5 changes the CLI ranking description from top-3 to top-5 while retaining Codex's 19.0% and Claude Code's 17.1%. v5 also adds domain/severity summaries and selected qualitative case findings, rather than performance gains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops mathematical theory or proofs. The vulnerability-boundary conditions and correctness/security classifications remain the same; the added mechanism explanations are qualitative.

C1.justification: v5 explicitly qualifies the abstract, contribution list and conclusion as concerning C/C++ memory-safety or memory-related vulnerabilities. v2 acknowledged this restriction in its limitations. This narrows the headline scope while retaining the benchmark's novelty claims and central finding of poor secure-coding performance.

C2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands explanations involving noisy or scarce security training data, scaffold priorities, context management and security workflows, and adds mitigation directions. Appendices B/E add applicability and failure-mechanism arguments. Section 7 adds source-dependent project bias, possible statistical instability and reasons naive SAST ensembles may amplify false alarms.

D1.justification: v5 adds GitHub and Hugging Face dataset links on the first page and accepted/rejected requirement examples in Appendix B. These improve access information and document existing filtering decisions. Hardware, software versions, agent budgets, requirement-generation model and prompt contents remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The comparisons with BaxBench, SusVibes and SecRepoBench and the positioning in Table 1 remain intact. v5 adds supporting literature on commit identification, vulnerability reports, static-analysis limitations, agent memory and safeguards. These additions broaden the supporting discussion without substantially redefining the work's relationship to its closest benchmarks.

P1.justification: v5 rewrites the title, adds a Features subsection and a separate Case Study appendix, and refines several explanations. Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. The original example and prompt appendices move from E/F to F/G, and unresolved prompt-figure references are fixed.

P2.justification: v5 replaces the two-column format with single-column pages, a styled title/abstract block and running headers, and extensively resizes and relocates tables, plots and code listings. It adds task-overview and construction diagrams in Figures 1–2 and the project-domain Table 5. Existing result plots and task examples are retained.

improvement.justification: v5 improves clarity and inspectability through explicit scope qualifications, code/data links, filtering examples, pipeline diagrams, corrected cross-references and additional case evidence. The gain is limited because the quantitative evidence and single-run design remain unchanged. Some new explanations about training data and general human–agent behavioral differences go beyond what the selected cases establish.
